data.title: Iran strikes on US diplomatic facilities in 4 Gulf countries cost $184M: IG report
data.description:
U.S. diplomatic facilities in four Gulf countries suffered around $184 million in estimated damages from Iranian military strikes, according to a new report from the Pentagon’s watchdog made public on Monday. 

The posts are located in Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE), the Pentagon watchdog said in the 44-page report, the first one since the U.S. and Israel launched the war in late February. 

The heaviest damage was sustained in Iraq with over $157 million in costs, followed by Kuwait with more than $14 million in damages and $11.5 million in Saudi Arabia, the report said. In the UAE, the U.S. diplomatic post suffered $125,000 in damages. The U.S. mission in Iraq experienced over 600 Iranian attacks. 

The Iranian military has targeted various U.S. military bases in the Gulf since Operation Epic Fury kicked off on Feb. 28, but Tehran has also inflicted heavy damages on diplomatic and intelligence outposts in those countries. 

From Feb. 28 to June 29, the Pentagon has estimated the cost of war to be $33.4 billion, but that does not include costs for infrastructure repairs.

In July, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told Senate lawmakers that the Iran war’s estimated cost was $37.5 billion, a sum that some experts argued was a low estimate. 

The State Department, meanwhile, reported that as of June 2, it had incurred $113 million in costs related to the war and “as it continues to assess damage, costs are likely to rise.”

In addition, 18 U.S. service members have been killed and some 800 wounded in the more than six-month war. About 50,000 American troops are still deployed to the region, with the Trump administration yet to provide a clear exit strategy from the deeply unpopular conflict. 

Top administration officials have at times downplayed the damages Iranian one-way attack drones and missiles have inflicted on U.S. military bases, aircraft and other assets in the U.S. Central Command (Centcom) theater. 

Last week, President Trump denied news reports that several U.S. military jets were damaged in Iran’s attack on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan. 

“None whatsoever. No damage. No nothing,” the president said in an interview with The Hill’s sister network NewsNation when asked about one A-10 Thunderbolt losing a wing and eight F-15s sustained light damage. 

More than 50 U.S. aircraft have been damaged or destroyed since the Iran war began, according to the watchdog’s report, including 4 F-15Es, seven KC-135 refueling aircraft, four AH-6 helicopters and at least 30 MQ-9 Reaper drones. 

But some top officials were more candid. 

“They blew the hell out of Bahrain,” the acting U.S. Navy secretary Hung Cao said in an interview last week with The Epoch Times when asked about the level of damage Naval Support Activity Bahrain (NASB), which serves as the headquarters for U.S. Naval Forces Central Command and the U.S. Fifth Fleet, had sustained since the conflict began. 

The Navy has used the NASB as its main logistics hub in the Middle East. The service branch is weighing what to do with the base, including if it should be repaired. 

“I have a task force that’s looking at that,” Cao said.

data.title: 6 takeaways as Trump takes sledgehammer to power plant climate regs
data.description:
The Trump administration on Monday gutted the rules governing the nation’s climate regulations for power plants. 

Here’s what you should know about the final rule from the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA):

It axes most, but not all, power plant climate rules

The rules, which have been announced but whose underlying text did not appear to be public at press time, are expected to ax most, but not all, of the climate regulations on the books for the power sector. 

When the Trump administration first proposed to get rid of Biden-era power plant rules last year, it said it would eliminate all climate rules for the sector.

Monday’s move stops short of immediately doing that. It gets rid of major components of past regulations but does leave a few pieces in place.

In particular, EPA Assistant Administrator Aaron Szabo told reporters that new natural gas plants would still need to abide by 2015 standards and 2024 efficiency requirements.

It also leaves in place Obama-era regulations for new coal power plants, though few if any new coal plants are expected to be built in the years ahead. 

It is joined by a proposal to eliminate all climate rules for the power sector in the future

The rule also comes with a supplemental proposal that, if finalized, would seek to repeal the agency’s authority to regulate power plants’ climate contributions entirely.

Szabo said the proposal would find that the Clean Air Act does not give the EPA the authority to regulate power plants’ planet-warming emissions.

In addition to axing the few regulations that remain, he said, the proposal could block future administrations from regulating power plants’ climate emissions.

If it’s finalized, a future administration could ultimately undo the maneuver, but in the meantime, it could act as a delay for future regulations. 

“Administrations are always free to change their mind and reinterpret statutes based on the best reading and based on the evidence before them,” said Meredith Hankins, federal climate legal director at the Natural Resources Defense Council. “It certainly just delays action. Every year that we continue to send unregulated carbon up into the atmosphere, that CO2 is sticking around, and it’s going to continue affecting climate change. It’s going to continue making extreme weather disasters worse.”

“These standards … require lead time. They need to give utilities time to plan, and they need regulatory certainty to think through ‘OK, what is our electricity mix going to look like 10 years from now, 20 years from now?’ And by delaying action, it’s just pushing those potential timelines back further and further, and it’s making it harder and harder for utilities to plan,” she added.

It is expected to mean significantly more emissions, worsening climate change

The proposal is expected to allow for significantly more planet-heating emissions such as carbon dioxide to be released into the atmosphere, worsening climate change.

A regulatory analysis of the Trump administration’s proposal, which does differ from the final rule, said that it would have allowed an estimated 38 million additional metric tons of carbon dioxide in 2028, an additional 50 million metric tons in 2030, 123 million metric tons in 2035, 54 million metric tons in 2040 and 42 million metric tons in 2045.

The U.S. power sector is a major driver of planet-warming emissions, responsible for a quarter of total U.S. emissions. 

A report from New York University School of Law’s Institute for Policy Integrity found that if the U.S. power sector were a country, it would be the world’s sixth-largest emitter, contributing more to climate change than the entirety of nations including Canada, Japan, Brazil and Mexico.

The report also said that the sector’s 2022 emissions alone will contribute to future climate change impacts that are expected to cause about 5,300 additional premature deaths in the U.S. due to heat and wildfire smoke.

“The public health and welfare toll of this deregulation is just going to be staggering,” said  Jason Schwartz, one of the report’s authors and regulatory policy director at the Institute, told The Hill.

The Biden-era rule that is now mostly repealed would have required existing coal plants and new gas plants to prevent 90 percent of their carbon dioxide emissions from entering the atmosphere. 

The Biden administration said that its rule would have prevented a total of 1.38 billion metric tons of carbon emissions through 2047, the equivalent of taking 328 million gas-powered cars off the road for a year.

It could have a modest impact on electricity prices

The change is expected to eventually lower electricity prices, but the changes may not be particularly dramatic.

An analysis based on the original proposal, from which the final rule slightly differs, found that in 2028 and 2030, the changes could actually increase average retail electricity prices by 0.7 percent and 0.5 percent, respectively.

In 2035, it would cause a 1.4 percent drop in electricity prices, as well as a 0.2 percent drop in 2040 and a 0.7 percent drop in 2045 compared to a baseline where the Biden-era regulation is not repealed. 

Trump administration officials touted the rule as cutting down power prices. 

“For over 15 years, the Obama and Biden administrations implemented a war on coal to destroy reliable and affordable energy. The Trump Administration has come in to protect American energy and to make sure you can afford to keep the lights on,” said EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin in a written statement. 

“Americans will see a decrease in electricity prices, but this is just the beginning,” he added.

It’s a big win for coal

The rule is expected to be a win for the coal sector, an industry that has been on the decline as other fuel sources, particularly natural gas, have become increasingly dominant. 

The analysis of last year’s proposal said that in 2028, coal production for use in the electric sector could be 6 percent higher than it otherwise would have been. By 2045, coal production would be expected to be 84 percent higher under last year’s proposal than it would have been if the Biden-era rules stayed in place.

In 2045, coal used by the power sector would have also been 32 percent more expensive under the proposal than it would have been under the Biden rule. 

A trade group representing the coal industry celebrated the regulation. 

Rich Nolan, president and CEO of the National Mining Association, said in a statement that the Trump rule “has averted what would have been a catastrophic collision of unlawful and unworkable Biden-era technology mandates with surging energy demands. “

“With today’s repeal, well-operating coal plants are no longer faced with the false choice between commercially unavailable and technically infeasible technologies, fuel-switching or closure. The administration’s action corrects the egregious misuse of the Clean Air Act as a political tool to end American coal generation and implements the law as Congress intended,” he added. 

Legal challenges are expected

Opponents of the Trump administration’s move are expected to sue to try to block it. 

“I would expect that the final repeal will be pretty immediately challenged,” said Dena Adler, senior attorney at the Institute for Policy Integrity. 

Some groups are already indicating they could sue. 

“The EPA has a legal obligation to protect us from climate pollution from power plants,” said Jill Tauber, vice president for climate and energy at Earthjustice, in a written statement. “Earthjustice and our partners will continue to defend climate protections and hold the Trump administration accountable.”

But, Adler said, it could take time before there’s any actual resolution. 

“It will be interesting to see how the litigation progresses because EPA is simultaneously finalizing a rule that assumes it has the authority to regulate greenhouse gas emissions, while also proposing it has no authority to regulate greenhouse gas emissions,” she said. 

“I think we’ll see immediate challenges, but I think we’re not going to necessarily get to the bottom of some of those legal claims until the intermediary question of EPA’s authority to regulate greenhouse gas emissions is addressed,” she added.

data.title: McConnell returns to Senate to cast first vote since June
data.description:
Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) returned to the Senate Monday evening to cast his first vote since June 11 after spending months away from the Capitol recuperating from a fall he suffered at home.

McConnell’s long absence and the trickle of information from his office about his condition fueled weeks of speculation about his health and whether he would return to the Senate before the end of his term in January.

“After two years, two decades, actually, of dodging your questions, I wasn’t sure how many of you would be here today. So I’m glad to see you. Time to get back to work, finish the job of this Congress,” McConnell told an assembled group of reporters outside the Senate chamber before casting a vote for Matthew Byrne, a nominee to serve as district judge for the Southern District of Ohio.

An aide pushed McConnell through the historic Ohio Clock Corridor in a wheelchair, where he appeared frail but in good spirits after three months away from his Senate colleagues.

“I’m here to work on the farm bill, it’s important to my state. And as I think you know I have an ongoing interest in NATO and backing up our good friends who are totally in a fight against the Russians,” he added, referring to Ukrainian forces who are grinding away at the front lines after more than four years of combat against invading Russian forces.

“Welcome back!” McConnell said to reporters, who returned to a busy schedule of votes after the five-week August recess.

McConnell was spotted earlier in the afternoon being wheeled out of his Capitol Hill townhouse by an aide and security detail while a crowd assembled on the sidewalk.

In a statement circulated by his office, McConnell said he was “really looking forward to being back on the Senate floor and seeing my colleagues.”

“My recovery has been a long and often frustrating process and the lingering effects of childhood polio haven’t made it any easier. I’m still not quite back to 100 percent but I’ve assured Leader Thuen that, as I continue with physical therapy on the advice of my doctors, I will do my best to be present for tough votes when our conference needs me,” he said.

McConnell return is a big relief to GOP senators as his presence will give them the votes they need to pass the farm bill out of the Agriculture Committee and to advance regular spending bills out of the Senate Appropriations Committee.

The farm bill stalled in the Agriculture Committee last month after Democrats voted along party lines against the legislation because of disagreements over cuts made to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) by Republicans in last year’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Republican leaders are reportedly aiming to try again to advance it this week.

McConnell, who is 84, was rushed to the hospital on June 14 after taking a fall at his Washington home.

His office announced he was discharged from the hospital in early August.

data.title: Newsom says he won't run for president in 2028 if Harris does
data.description:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) said in an interview on Monday that he wouldn’t run for president in 2028 if former Vice President Kamala Harris ran for a third bid, pointing out that they’d both be fighting over similar bases of supporters. 

“First of all, electorally, it’s a gift from God for everybody else. They’d enjoy the hell out of it,” Newsom told CNN’s Jake Tapper while fly fishing in Montana. “Mutual assured destruction. It services no greater good.” 

When Tapper offered the counter argument that Harris had won twice and lost while Newsom had never ran before, the California governor argued that they’d split their share of primary voters if the two ran against each other. 

“I know her base of supporters. I know her friends,” Newsom said. “The [Venn] diagram on that is just pure crossover.” 

“I wouldn’t do that to people,” he added. 

Newsom is widely floated as a potential 2028 White House candidate and is mulling a possible run. Harris, who also hails from California and shares a similar political orbit with Newsom, is as well. 

The California governor’s interview marks the first time that he’s addressed forgoing a White House bid if his Golden State counterpart were to join the 2028 primary mix. 

Many potential hopefuls on either side are expected to start announcing decisions after the November midterms.  

Newsom has been traveling to states like South Carolina and Michigan, while Harris has traveled across the country as a part of her book tour while weighing in on the midterm races.  

Having two Californians — potentially three, with Rep. Ro Khanna — could be a risky bet for Democrats not only because they would share the same political home, but hailing from the reliably blue state could make it harder to bring in independents or disaffected Republicans.

data.title: Cruz: Trump should sign college sports bill live on ESPN's 'College GameDay' once passed
data.description:
Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) told reporters he would like to see the Protect College Sports Act, the proposed landmark legislation regulating the big business of college sports, signed by President Trump live on ESPN’s “College GameDay.”

“Our goal from the beginning was not just to squeak by with 60 votes but to get a big bipartisan vote. We got that in committee, which surprised a lot of observers,” Cruz said during a press conference outside the Capitol on Monday. “I’ve spoken with House leadership in the last week and if we get a big bipartisan vote, it goes into the House with a lot of momentum … and the president is ready to sign it.”

Cruz grinned as he floated an unusual venue for the president to sign the legislation should it pass both chambers of Congress.

“I’ve actually suggested that he sign it on ‘College Gameday,’ on campus, which truly would be a remarkable moment,” the senator said, in reference to ESPN’s popular college football pregame show. “We’ve gotta get there first, but it would be an amazing victory for student athletes if we can get that done.”

The bipartisan group of lawmakers has been telegraphing confidence in the bill’s chances for weeks, pointing to recent controversies in college football and basketball regarding player eligibility and compensation as evidence the “wild west” of college sports needs to be better regulated.

The sweeping bipartisan legislation would grant the NCAA and its member schools limited antitrust protection shielding it from litigation around issues like the transfer portal, revenue sharing and student-athlete compensation through name, image and likeness endorsement deals.

Trump has endorsed the Protect College Sports Act, following the formation of a White House Task Force on College Sports earlier this year and an executive order he signed with language that closely mirrors key points of the Protect College Sports Act.

Some of the bill’s backers have expressed worry that Trump’s attachment to the bill could hurt its chances with Democrats before the midterm elections this fall.

“The president is enthusiastic, but he’s also given space in the Senate to let the coalition come together,” Cruz said. “With some senators, the president’s endorsement is more helpful than with others. That’s the nature of politics, and he understands that.”

Monday’s presser came just days after Cruz appeared on “College GameDay” to advocate with the bill, during which he was met with boos from fans at the University of Texas as he spoke extensively about the legislation.

Legendary Alabama coach Nick Saban, also a co-host of ESPN’s “College GameDay,” is one of the bill’s most prominent backers.

Critics of the College Sports Act, including Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.), contend the bill hands the NCAA and top universities too much power and will limit the earning potential of most student athletes, particularly at nonrevenue-generating and Olympic sports.

Some conservative members in the Senate, meanwhile, have expressed concern about the bill’s ramifications relating to transgender athletes, particularly in states where they are banned from competition.

A vote on the bill, authored by Cruz and Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), is expected as soon as Tuesday, though the lawmakers said Monday it could be pushed to next week depending on how efforts to whip votes in the upper chamber progress this week.

data.title: As AI fears spike, Trump bats down calls for regulation
data.description:
President Trump is downplaying the growing concerns about artificial intelligence and resisting calls for regulation, putting him out of step with a growing chorus of concerns coming from within the tech industry and both sides of the political aisle.

Trump, speaking with reporters over the weekend and in social media posts on Monday, said warnings about AI going rogue and endangering humanity were overblown. 

“We can put guardrails, we can do this and that, but I think you have a lot of negative forces that are bringing it up that … shouldn’t be bringing it up, and they’re bringing up things that won’t happen,” Trump said. 

The president doubled down on his position in a TruthSocial post on Monday, defending his approach and calling out Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who warned of the dangers of unchecked AI in a blog post over the weekend. 

“The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” the president wrote. In a second post, he called the fear of AI destroying humanity a “hoax.”

Stocks plummeted in response to growing calls for AI regulation on Monday, with the Nasdaq Composite Index falling 0.9 percent and the S&P 500 dropping 0.6 percent.

Industry officials beyond Amodei have also weighed in. OpenAI’s Sam Altman wrote in an X post that the “world deserves confidence that American companies developing increasingly capable AI will act responsibly, especially as the trajectory of progress has steepened.”

“We welcome a federal framework that sets consistent safety requirements for frontier AI,” he wrote.

Elon Musk, one of Trump’s closest allies in the tech world, said, “Dario is right,” in a post on X this weekend.  

Trump and his allies argue that less regulation on AI is essential for Washington to win the AI race against Beijing. 

“He is very much a trust the plan, trust the system, trust the markets, trust the innovators kind of guy,” said Chris Johnson, a Republican strategist and president of the American Energy Leadership Institute. 

“There are two groups of people: there are Americans and panicans, and you don’t want to be a panican,” he said. 

But the hands-off approach to AI regulation threatens to open the president up to political blowback as Americans grow increasingly concerned about AI and the data centers that power the technology. 

Seventy-eight percent of likely voters said they would choose “mandatory standards” on AI while only eight percent said they chose “no regulation,” according to a poll released in June from the nonpartisan AI Policy Institute. 

“I do think that Republicans are going to talk more and more about AI safety and security. The polling data on this is really clear,” said Brendan Steinhauser, a Texas-based Republican strategist and CEO of the Alliance to Secure AI. 

“I see the political winds shifting on this in favor of more regulation, and I’m confident that the White House, the Speaker [Mike Johnson (R-La.)], and [Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-N.D.)] are going to get together with the companies and find some way to move forward to pace development, and to put at least some safeguards on the technology,” he continued. 

The warnings come as Congress heads back into session for the final time before November’s midterm elections. Johnson said Monday that the White House will host a meeting with AI executives as soon as this week to “sort this out.”

AI has emerged as a top issue on the campaign trail, with Democrats and Republicans calling for guardrails. 

In Michigan, Democratic senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed has called for “public oversight” on AI, while Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R ) has enacted regulations on AI data centers in his own state. 

“We are on an exponential growth curve in AI,” Steinhauser said. “This issue is not going to recede.”

“You can see by January or February of next year when the presidential cycle kicks off anyway, you’re going to see every candidate talking about this,” he continued. 

Vice President Vance, a leading potential 2028 contender, urged caution on the issue while speaking to reporters on Monday. 

“I feel a little bit weird about the fact that we have so many frontier AI tech companies’ kind of talking to the government and begging the government to regulate them. It feels a little bit to me like a bit of a trojan horse, so I think we just have to be careful about this,” Vance said, noting that there are “risks” and “benefits” to the technology. 

Trump and other proponents of AI data centers argue they are essential to the country’s national security and development, while opponents point to the financial and environmental costs. 

Doug Kelly, CEO of the tech industry group American Edge Group, which promotes data centers, noted that China leads the U.S. in energy, adoption, and talent for AI, but that the U.S. still holds an advantage in infrastructure and chips. 

“We can’t give up our strongest advantage. We need to be able to build more data centers, manufacture more advanced chips, and develop the world’s best AI models here in America,” Kelly said. 

Will Rinehard, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, said the Chinese “are definitely very, very, very closely monitoring what’s happening in America because we have an incredible bench of talent.”

But he said he doesn’t see the implementation of guardrails significantly slowing progress.

The AI guardrail conversation has brought together some unlikely allies. Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders (I) and former White House adviser Steve Bannon are set to speak at the same Pro-Human Assembly event on Tuesday to push for human-controlled AI.

Jessica Brandt, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, said “the future will favor a paired approach.”

“National security policies that maximize the U.S. lead over China are essential to ensuring AI doesn’t tip the balance of power against us,” she said. “They also buy time to build a domestic regulatory framework that ensures AI is developed and deployed in ways that are safe and broadly beneficial.”

Others say they see an emerging dividing line between Republicans and Democrats on AI. 

“You can always peel off a few people from the other side and find ways to make them sympathetic to your point,” said Johnson of the American Energy Leadership Institute. “I think generally Republicans and conservatives broadly are going to be much more in line with the president.” 

“If you’re somebody who’s in the tech industry or in the tech policy space, you need to start waking up real quick to who’s on team red versus who’s on team blue,” he added.

data.title: Costco nearly doubles cost of motor oil, limits purchases
data.description:
(NEXSTAR) — Costco may have cut the prices for several popular items earlier this year, but it’s now raising the cost and limiting the sale of another: motor oil.

Costco’s Kirkland Signature full-synthetic motor oil 5-quart two pack now costs around $58, well above the approximately $30 it had been selling for just last year, and limiting customers to buying two boxes a week. It is also limiting purchases of Mobil 1’s full-synthetic motor oil 1-quart six pack, which sells for about $44, to five per membership.

A price hike and purchase limits may take you back to the days of empty shelves where toilet paper once stood, but this likely won’t impact you as much as you may immediately fear.

Unless you’re responsible for “a fleet of thousands of cars,” you probably don’t have to worry about it much, Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis for GasBuddy, told Nexstar.

“The normal car requires four to five quarts every 5,000 miles or so,” De Haan said, describing Costco’s limit as “what would be an extremely reasonable amount.”

It is, however, indicative of a larger picture: high oil prices.

De Haan told Nexstar that oil prices have reached their highest level in months. He pointed to attacks in the Middle East, the Red Sea, and the East-West Crude Oil Pipeline in Saudi Arabia, as well as Ukrainian drone attacks against Russian oil refineries, as contributing to the price hikes. The Saudi oil pipeline will mostly be out of service for weeks following an attack last week, two regional officials told The Associated Press.

The price for a barrel of Brent crude went above $109 on Monday morning.

“As you would expect, everything derived from a barrel of oil is being impacted in different ways,” De Haan said.

While Costco’s motor oil price hikes and sale limits may not impact you much, you may continue to feel pressure at the pump, especially if you drive a diesel vehicle.

The national average for a gallon of regular gasoline, as of Sept. 14, is $4.31, according to AAA. That’s well over the $3.17 per gallon average reported at this time last year.

Diesel, meanwhile, set a record on Monday, with a national average of $6.23, per AAA data. At this time last year, the national average was just under $3.70 per gallon.

Prices at the pump for diesel and regular gasoline closely follow that of crude oil.

With oil prices continuing to rise due to ongoing tension in the Middle East, oil companies stand to profit more from turning refined crude oil into diesel or gasoline than motor oil.

It remains to be seen if other motor oil retailers like Walmart, Amazon and AutoZone will boost their prices or set purchase limits. Walmart, Amazon and AutoZone did not immediately respond to requests for comment from The Associated Press.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

data.title: Trump nominates Wesley Hunt to Saudi Arabia ambassador post
data.description:
President Trump on Monday nominated Rep. Wesley Hunt (R-Texas) to serve as U.S. ambassador to Saudi Arabia.

Trump sent the nominations of Hunt and a slew of other individuals to the Senate, which has to confirm his appointments.

The U.S. has not had a full-time ambassador to Saudi Arabia since Michael Ratney left office at the end of the Biden administration. Jennifer Larson, a career member of the State Department’s Foreign Service, has led the U.S. Embassy in Riyadh on an interim basis since mid-August — succeeding Alison Dilworth.

Hunt is departing the lower chamber after two terms representing Texas’s 38th Congressional District. The 44-year-old former Army officer finished third in the Lone Star State’s Senate GOP primary in March, a race state Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) won via runoff over incumbent Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas).

The Texas representative is set to leave the House at the end of his term in January. In a statement, Hunt said it was the “honor of a lifetime” for Trump to nominate him to the ambassadorship post.

“Having served in the region both in combat as an Army officer and for two years as a diplomatic liaison in the Kingdom, I understand the strategic importance of the partnership between the United States and Saudi Arabia and the profound responsibility of this position,” Hunt said.

“When confirmed, I will serve with humility and honor, advance his vision of peace through strength and deepen this vital partnership,” he added.

The Hill has reached out to a Hunt spokesperson regarding whether the GOP lawmaker will resign from the House, if confirmed.

Trump and his family have business ties to Saudi Arabia, and the president has a close relationship with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman — whom U.S. intelligence said “approved” the 2018 operation that resulted in the murder of journalist Jamal Khashoggi.

Last month, the Trump administration sent a nuclear cooperation agreement with Saudi Arabia to Congress. Under the 30-year deal, U.S. companies would be able to develop the kingdom’s civil nuclear infrastructure.

The president has stipulated, though, that Saudi Arabia must normalize ties with Israel for the deal to take effect.

data.title: Trump guts climate rules for coal and gas power plants
data.description:
The Trump administration on Monday gutted regulations that limited planet-warming emissions from coal- and gas-fired power plants. 

The move allows a sector that makes up a large share of the U.S.’s climate change contributions to release greenhouse gases unchecked by the government. It’s expected to be a win for the fossil fuel industry, while allowing the release of significantly more planet-heating pollution.

When it proposed to kill the regulations entirely last year, the Trump administration estimated that in the year 2035 alone, this would result in the release of 123 million more metric tons of carbon dioxide, equivalent to putting an additional 28.7 million gas-powered cars on the road.

Monday’s move could be slightly different. While it is expected to repeal large swaths of Biden-era power plant regulations, Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) assistant administrator Aaron Szabo told reporters that limited pieces of Biden- and Obama-era regs would remain in place. 

In addition to Monday’s final rule, the EPA proposed to find that the Clean Air Act does not give it the authority to regulate power plant emissions due to their climate impacts. If finalized, Szabo said that this move could block future administrations from regulating power plants’ climate emissions. 

Overall, he said that the moves would allow “American families and businesses experience lower electricity costs … thanks to an increased power supply.”

The moves come as high electricity demand and increasing power prices continue to be a major political issue. Last year’s analysis found that in 2035, axing power plant climate rules could reduce electricity prices by an average of 1.4 percent.

In a press release, the EPA said that it expects its final rule to save $310 billion.

President Trump has falsely said that climate change is a “hoax” on multiple occasions, and his administration has broadly sought to cut back or eliminate climate regulations. It recently repealed all climate rules for cars and trucks, saying their emissions did not pose a threat to the public.

Climate change has been linked to worsening heat waves and extreme weather. The U.S. power sector is a major driver of planet-warming emissions, responsible for a quarter of total U.S. emissions. 

Environmental activists recoiled at the Trump administration’s latest rollback before news of it was officially announced.

“It’s really just the Trump EPA putting their head in the sand,” said Meredith Hankins, federal climate legal director at the Natural Resources Defense Council. “I mean, you can look at the weather we experienced this summer, the heat waves on the Fourth of July. We’re going into an El Niño season with potential hurricanes and even more extreme weather. We see the impacts of climate change all around us every day, and the Trump EPA is trying to say, ‘Well, that’s not our problem.'”

Meanwhile, industry players celebrated the move.

Rachael Marsh, chief legal officer at the Edison Electric Institute, a trade group representing power companies, said in a statement that it “welcomes EPA’s repeal” of the Biden-era rule. 

The EPA’s action repeals most of a Biden-era rule that would have required existing coal plants and new gas plants to prevent 90 percent of their carbon dioxide emissions from entering the atmosphere.

data.title: Jeffries calls on Congress to stay in Washington to address AI concerns
data.description:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) is calling on House GOP leaders to remain in Washington to allow Congress to consider new limits on AI companies following dire warnings from industry insiders about the threat the technology poses to humanity. 

Speaking to reporters Monday in the Capitol, Jeffries said the calls for a slowdown from within the industry should be a wakeup call for lawmakers in the Capitol, who have dabbled at the edges of AI regulation for years without taking any significant steps to ensure public safety.

Jeffries did not promote specific reforms, but urged Congress to delay its long, pre-election recess “until something is done decisively to protect the safety and the well-being of the American people.”

“Republicans have completely abandoned their responsibility to legislate and engage in public policy efforts in a responsible fashion in the area of artificial intelligence,” Jeffries said.

The pressure is unlikely to bear fruit. Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) opposes any swift action on new AI regulations, warning that hasty new limits risk overburdening American technology companies to the benefit of America’s global adversaries. 

“The reflex of legislative bodies is to cover things up with red tape and in hyperregulation,” Johnson told reporters Monday in the Capitol. “If you do that, then you lose your edge.”

Johnson has scheduled the House to adjourn on Thursday and remain in recess through the Nov. 3 elections.

Still, the public anxieties surrounding AI — and the related issue of data centers, which are helping to fuel the AI boom — have increasingly become campaign fodder heading into the midterms, when both the House and Senate are up for grabs. 

The issue reached new heights over the weekend when three top leaders in the AI industry — Dario Amodei, Elon Musk and Sam Altman — urged a more cautious approach to the development of the technology. A failure to do so, Amodei, the head of Anthropic, warned in a long blog post, could lead to global catastrophe. 

President Trump has come out strongly in favor of data centers and against regulating AI — two positions that put him at odds with the majority of voters. And Democrats are highlighting both topics to portray the president and other GOP leaders as out of touch with public sentiment heading to the polls. 

“They’re not really concerned about over-regulation. They want no regulation,” Jeffries said. “And that’s the height of irresponsibility.” 

Jeffries noted that, in the previous Congress, he and former Speaker Kevin McCarthy (R-Calif.) had launched an AI task force designed to balance the success of American AI companies with public safety precautions. The panel did not survive the transition into the new Congress — a development Jeffries blamed on Trump’s return to the White House.

“Republicans in this Congress, at the direction of Donald Trump, detonated that bipartisan effort and endangered the health and the safety and the well-being of the American people in doing so,” he said.
